name: Bengaluru Outer Ring Road
lanes: 6–8 lanes with service roads, grade-separated at the main junctions
history: The Outer Ring Road was laid out in the 1990s as a bypass around what was then the edge of Bengaluru, and the city promptly grew straight past it. Within fifteen years the stretch between Hebbal, K. R. Puram, Marathahalli and Silk Board had become the address of choice for technology parks, and today more office workers travel this one road than any other in the city. Flyovers and underpasses were added at the worst junctions, and a metro line is being built along the eastern arc, but the road remains the definition of a Bengaluru traffic jam.
facts: Built in the 1990s to bypass Bengaluru; the city grew past it within a decade.
The Hebbal–Marathahalli–Silk Board stretch carries a large share of the city's technology-park commute.
The companies along it formed their own association to lobby about the traffic on it.
A metro line is being built along part of the corridor to take pressure off it.
The Silk Board junction at its southern end is one of the most notorious road junctions in India.
significance: Bengaluru's technology industry grew along this road rather than in the old city centre, so the ORR is where a very large share of the city's jobs are. What happens to traffic on it decides how long a million commutes take.

travelNotes: Avoid the eastern arc between 8.30 and 11 in the morning and from 5 to 9 in the evening if you can. Service roads run alongside for most of the length and are often quicker for short hops.
